blocks.title: Damped oscillations
blocks.text: Oscillations whose amplitude decreases because of resistive forces are called damped oscillations, and the resistive forces are called damping forces.

In an ideal free oscillation the total mechanical energy stays constant, as for the mass-spring system, a body moving in a circle and a simple pendulum. In practice, dissipating forces such as air resistance and friction act, so the amplitude decreases gradually with time and the body finally comes to rest. For example, a girl on a swing oscillates with smaller and smaller amplitude and eventually stops (Fig 14.14); the damped oscillation is shown on a graph in Fig 14.15. A swinging pendulum slowly coming to rest, and an oscillating tuning fork touched with a finger, are other examples.

blocks.alt: A swing on its frame shown at successive extreme positions on alternate sides, each closer to the vertical than the last, with three arcs below it getting shorter. A panel explains that air resistance and friction take energy away on every swing, so the amplitude decreases until the swing comes to rest; this is light damping.
blocks.caption: Damped oscillation of a swing: each swing smaller than the last (original diagram after Fig 14.14).
blocks.long_description: Resistive forces do work against the motion on every swing, so the energy and the amplitude fall step by step. A playground swing is lightly damped: it oscillates many times before it stops.

items: Light damping: the energy and amplitude decrease gradually. A playground swing is a good example.
Heavy damping: the body takes a long time to return to rest, for example a pendulum in thick oil.
Critical damping: the body returns to its equilibrium position in the shortest possible time, for example the shock absorbers of a car.

blocks.alt: Top: a damped oscillation; a blue curve oscillates about the time axis with peaks that shrink inside a dashed envelope. Bottom: displacement against time after release for three cases: light damping (blue) oscillates with slowly shrinking swings; critical damping (green) returns to zero fastest without crossing it; heavy damping (red) drops slowly towards zero without oscillating. A note says car shock absorbers are designed close to critical damping.
blocks.caption: Damped oscillations and light, critical and heavy damping (original graphs; the top graph is after Fig 14.15).
blocks.long_description: Damping takes energy out of the oscillation. Too little damping leaves the body bouncing; too much makes it creep back slowly; critical damping brings it back to rest in the shortest time.

blocks.text: Shock absorbers in the suspension system of a car are a practical application of damping. Damping is needed for a comfortable ride when a car moves on a bumpy, rough road: without it the car would keep bouncing after every bump.

blocks.alt: A schematic of a car's suspension: the car body at the top joined to the wheel below by a coil spring and, beside it, a shock absorber, a piston that moves through oil inside a cylinder. The wheel stands on a bumpy road. A panel explains that the spring takes up the bump and the shock absorber does work against the oil, so the oscillation dies away quickly.
blocks.caption: Suspension of a vehicle: a coil spring and a shock absorber (original schematic after Fig 14.16).
blocks.long_description: After a bump the spring would let the car keep bouncing; the shock absorber turns that energy into heat in the oil. Near-critical damping brings the car body back to its normal level quickly without oscillating.
